body.x: Families arranging a Shia nikah for the first time often ask the same question: what actually happens, and in what order? The ceremony is shorter and simpler than most people expect, but the steps around it — agreeing the mahr, arranging representatives, sorting the paperwork — reward a little preparation. Here is the procedure as it usually unfolds, from the decision to the feast.

Nothing in the aqd itself is negotiated on the day. Before a date is set, the couple and their families have already agreed the essentials: that both parties consent freely; who the bride's wali is, and that his permission is in place where it is required; and the mahr — its amount or nature, and how it is divided between the portion given at the contract and any deferred portion. Many families also discuss practical conditions the couple may wish to record in the contract itself, such as arrangements about where they will live: conditions written into a Shia marriage contract are binding on both sides, so this conversation deserves real time. Some families consult their marja's office at this stage with any questions of validity, and many couples perform istikhara — a prayer seeking guidance — before finalising, as a spiritual step rather than a procedural one.
Stage two: the day itself, step by step

Gathering and sermon — guests assemble, and the officiant or reciter opens with a short sermon (khutba) and recitation from the Quran, often including the verses that speak of marriage and the tranquillity between spouses.
Confirming consent and permission — the officiant confirms that the bride consents to the marriage and that the wali's permission has been given where it is required; in many communities the bride is asked through her representative.
Appointing the representatives — if the couple are not reciting the formula themselves, each side's wakil is named: one to speak for the bride, one for the groom.
Stating the mahr — the agreed mahr is announced clearly, so that it forms part of the contract wording that follows.
The offer — the bride's side recites the ijab, the offer of marriage, in Arabic and in the prescribed form, naming both parties and the mahr.
The acceptance — the groom's side immediately recites the qabul, accepting the marriage on those terms, in the same sitting, with no interval between offer and acceptance.
Witnessing and congratulations — the witnesses attest to what was recited, and the couple are now husband and wife. Prayers are made for them; in many communities sweets are distributed and the families embrace.
Signing — the written marriage contract, often called the nikah nama or aqd certificate, is signed by the couple, the representatives, the witnesses and the officiant.

The whole sequence commonly takes well under an hour, and the contract portion itself only a few minutes. Its brevity is not carelessness: everything debatable was settled in stage one, so that the recitation can be exact, calm and uninterrupted.
Choosing the setting and the officiant

The aqd can be held wherever the family is comfortable: a mosque or Islamic centre, a family home, a hired hall, or occasionally outdoors. Centres often have a scholar or reciter who performs contracts regularly and will walk the family through the wording in advance; for a home ceremony, families invite a scholar they know or ask their centre for a recommendation. Whoever officiates, agree beforehand who the two witnesses will be, who will act as wakil for each side if representatives are being used, and whether the bride will be present in the room or nearby with her representative — both arrangements are common, and the choice is the family's. A short rehearsal of names, including their correct pronunciation and the exact form of the mahr, prevents the only awkwardness the ceremony ever really has: a pause in the middle of the formula.
Stage three: the paperwork that makes it official twice over

The religious contract is one record; the state keeps another. How the two connect depends entirely on where you marry. In some countries the religious officiant is state-licensed, and the same signing registers the marriage in law. In others — much of Europe and North America, for example — a nikah alone is not a legal marriage, and the couple must also complete a civil registration or ceremony for the state to recognise them as spouses, with real consequences for inheritance, next-of-kin rights and children if they do not. Couples marrying across borders should also plan ahead for certified copies and, where needed, translations of the contract document, since embassies and immigration authorities ask for paperwork in their own formats. Keep the signed original somewhere safe; families routinely need it years later.
After the aqd: the walima and the first days

The walima is the feast that announces the marriage, traditionally hosted by the groom's side after the contract. Some families hold it the same evening; others separate the aqd and the celebrations by weeks or months, and during that interval the couple are fully married in religious law, even while living arrangements follow the family's own plan. Photographs, the bride's formal entry and the long guest list belong to these celebrations rather than to the contract ceremony itself. What matters procedurally is already done: consent given, mahr agreed and recorded, the formula recited, witnesses present, signatures on paper.

Seen end to end, the Shia nikah is deliberately uncomplicated: agree honestly, recite carefully, record properly. The searching and getting to know one another that precede it are where the time goes — and where Shia Rishta is designed to help, with family involvement, private photos and conversations that open only on mutual interest, so that couples arrive at this procedure with the agreement already built.

excerpt: From the first agreement and the setting of the mahr to the recitation of the aqd, the signing, and the walima — the Shia nikah in the order it actually happens.
title: Shia nikah procedure step by step
